taxonomyNote: NatureServe treats A. piscivorus as a species without subspecies and elevates A. conanti (Florida cottonmouth) to a separate species, calling the present one Northern Cottonmouth; ADW's account is titled A. piscivorus (conanti) and includes Florida within its range.
fieldMarks: Heavy-bodied venomous snake, to about 1.8 m; adults olive, brown or black with dark, dumbbell-shaped crossbands that are darker at the edges and lighter in the centre, blackening toward the tail.
Large spade-shaped head, brown, black or olive on top, with brown patches on the chin; inside of the mouth is bright white.
Juveniles are brighter with more distinct crossbands and a yellow tail tip.
Males are longer and heavier than females.
behavior: Threat display: shakes the tail, raises the head a few inches, coils and gapes to show the white mouth; also emits a foul musk.
Mostly nocturnal but may bask by day; adults stay within about 500 m of water; most active roughly March-November in the Carolinas and inactive in cold weather.
Eats fishes, amphibians, reptiles, small mammals, birds and carrion; gives live birth to 1-16 young, mainly August-September.
habitat: Wide range of aquatic and wetland habitats: swamps, sloughs, bayous, ponds and streams in pine flatwoods, marshes, river bottoms, floodplains, tidal stream courses and sometimes brackish water.
Winters in rocky hillsides, crayfish burrows, stumps or mammal burrows.
range: NatureServe lists the species in Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Kentucky, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas; Florida populations are assigned to A. conanti in that source.
